approaches.name: Direct subcutaneous approach to the ulnar shaft
approaches.corridor: Along the subcutaneous ulnar border through the interval between flexor carpi ulnaris and extensor carpi ulnaris

sources.title: Exposure of the forearm and distal radius

procedure_applications.condition: Direct plate fixation or reconstruction of the middle or distal ulnar shaft is required
The ulna requires a separate direct exposure in addition to the selected radial approach

positioning.text: Position according to the accompanying radial procedure; for isolated ulna exposure, maintain neutral rotation with the forearm accessible across the torso, on a side table, or vertical with the elbow supported.

setup.text: Prepare the whole limb for forearm rotation and choose a position that preserves access to a separate radial incision when both bones require fixation.

surface_landmarks.text: Mark the olecranon tip, palpable subcutaneous border of the ulna, ulnar styloid, and the required shaft segment.

incision.text: Incise longitudinally along the subcutaneous border from the olecranon toward the ulnar styloid, limiting length to the exposure required; when severe swelling threatens closure, place the incision slightly over adjacent extensor muscle so an open wound does not leave an implant directly exposed.

superficial_interval.text: Raise limited full-thickness flaps from the subcutaneous ulnar border and identify the fascia over flexor carpi ulnaris and extensor carpi ulnaris.

deep_interval.text: Develop the internervous interval between flexor carpi ulnaris and extensor carpi ulnaris directly onto the ulna.

layers.text: Skin, thin subcutaneous tissue, forearm fascia, flexor carpi ulnaris–extensor carpi ulnaris interval, periosteum, then ulna.

structures_encountered.text: The subcutaneous ulnar border, flexor carpi ulnaris, extensor carpi ulnaris, periosteum, and ulnar shaft are encountered; the dorsal sensory branch of the ulnar nerve enters the distal field.

structures_at_risk.text: The dorsal sensory branch of the ulnar nerve distally, ulnar neurovascular structures with excessive volar dissection, extensor and flexor muscle attachments, and vulnerable subcutaneous skin are at risk.

danger_zones.text: During distal extension, identify and protect the dorsal sensory branch of the ulnar nerve as it crosses toward the dorsum of the hand.

retraction_hazards.text: Limit circumferential stripping and avoid forceful volar retraction that threatens the ulnar neurovascular bundle or fracture blood supply.

exposure.text: Provides direct extensile access to the middle and distal ulnar shaft and can be lengthened proximally or distally as pathology requires.

limitations.text: The implant and bone have little soft-tissue cover, distal extension threatens the dorsal sensory branch, and marked swelling can prevent safe primary closure.

extensions.text: Extend along the subcutaneous border toward the olecranon or ulnar styloid while reassessing nerve anatomy and skin viability at each end.

indications.text: Use for direct fixation, debridement, grafting, or reconstruction of the ulnar shaft and for the ulnar component of selected both-bone forearm procedures.

relative_contraindications.text: Modify or defer the approach when the ulnar skin is compromised, swelling precludes closure, or previous scarring makes the direct subcutaneous corridor unsafe.

implant_implications.text: Select a plate position that respects the subcutaneous soft-tissue envelope and minimizes symptomatic prominence while preserving fracture biology.

fluoroscopy_implications.text: Confirm ulnar length, alignment, rotation, plate position, screw containment, and proximal and distal radioulnar-joint congruity on orthogonal views.

closure.text: Close fascia and skin without nerve entrapment or tension; if swelling prevents safe coverage, use a staged wound-management strategy rather than closing over pressure.

complications.text: Complications include dorsal ulnar sensory neuropathy, wound breakdown, symptomatic hardware, infection, compartment syndrome, radioulnar synostosis, malunion, and nonunion.

bailouts.text: If skin cannot cover the implant without tension, alter the incision over a muscular bed when planned preoperatively or use staged soft-tissue management rather than forced primary closure.

questions.question: What is the deep interval for the direct ulnar approach?
questions.answer: Between flexor carpi ulnaris and extensor carpi ulnaris.

questions.question: Which nerve is endangered by distal extension?
questions.answer: The dorsal sensory branch of the ulnar nerve.

questions.question: Why might a swollen forearm change incision placement?
questions.answer: An incision over adjacent extensor muscle leaves a muscular bed if safe primary closure is impossible.
